problemText: Humanism, the central intellectual program of the Renaissance, was built on the close study and recovery of which body of writing?
choices: Classical Greek and Roman texts
Chinese Confucian classics
Norse sagas and Icelandic poetry
Newly written reports of laboratory experiments
hints: Petrarch spent his life hunting through church libraries for forgotten manuscripts written centuries before his own time, in Latin.

problemText: The Medici, a Florentine banking family with no noble ancestry, paid for a family chapel, large sculptures, and a public library. Historians call this practice patronage. What does the term mean?
choices: A church tax collected from every artist's workshop in a city, with the money used to pay for new cathedrals and chapels
A guild rule requiring master artists to train apprentices without pay in exchange for the right to sell their work
Wealthy individuals or institutions paying artists and scholars to produce work, often gaining prestige in return
A royal decree declaring that all art made in a city belonged to the crown rather than to the artists who produced it
hints: Ask who hands over the money and what they expect to receive besides the object itself.

problemText: Medieval European painters often sized figures according to holy importance and set them against flat gold backgrounds. Renaissance painters instead built convincing three-dimensional space on a flat surface. Which technique was most responsible for that change?
choices: Linear perspective, in which parallel lines converge toward a vanishing point
Fresco painting applied to wet plaster so that colors bonded with the wall
Grinding gold leaf into pigment to give backgrounds a deeper, richer shine
Illuminated lettering copied from monastic manuscript workshops into panels
hints: The problem the artists were solving was depth: how to make a floor recede and a building sit behind a figure.

problemText: A bookseller in a German city wrote in the 1490s (paraphrased): 'In my grandfather's day one Bible cost as much as a vineyard and took a copyist two years to finish. This season I sold forty copies out of my shop and still have stock on the shelf.' Which development does this account most directly document?
choices: The founding of Europe's first universities, which created a new demand for books
The arrival of Byzantine scholars in Italy carrying Greek manuscripts
The spread of printing with movable type, which turned books from luxury items into affordable goods
A collapse in the price of farmland that made vineyards cheap
hints: Compare the two numbers he gives: how long one book took to produce, versus how many he now sells at once.

problemText: In 1453 the Ottomans captured Constantinople, the Byzantine capital. Historians have long linked that event to the growth of Renaissance learning in Italy. What is the connection?
choices: Ottoman rulers commissioned Italian painters for the new imperial court, and those painters carried new styles back into Italy on their return
Byzantine scholars moved west carrying Greek manuscripts of writers such as Plato, Aristotle, and Euclid that western Europe had largely lost
The fall destroyed Italian banking houses that had lent to the Byzantines, so merchants put their remaining money into art instead
Italian cities gained direct overland control of the Asian spice trade, and the new profits paid for schools and libraries across the peninsula
hints: Ask what a fleeing scholar would carry with him, and what Italian humanists most wanted to get their hands on.

problemText: A student argues that the Renaissance shows Europeans abandoning religion in favor of reason. All four statements below are historically accurate. Which one most directly weakens that argument?
choices: Renaissance painters mastered linear perspective and studied anatomy from real bodies, sometimes dissecting corpses to understand how muscles and bones fit together
Printing with movable type made books cheap enough for ordinary townspeople to buy, and the number of books in circulation multiplied within a few decades
Renaissance writers coined the label 'Dark Ages' for the centuries before their own, presenting their age as a revival of classical learning
Churches and devout patrons commissioned most Renaissance art, its subjects stayed largely religious, and leading humanists such as Erasmus were churchmen
hints: Three of these are true but say nothing at all about belief — look for the one that speaks to who paid for the art and what the art showed.
Ask whether humanism replaced Christian faith or added attention to this life alongside it.

problemText: In October 1517 a monk and university professor at Wittenberg circulated a list of ninety-five points for academic debate, many of them objecting to the sale of indulgences. Who was he?
choices: John Calvin
Martin Luther
Erasmus of Rotterdam
Ignatius of Loyola
hints: He was a German monk, and the emperor outlawed him at the Diet of Worms in 1521.

problemText: In 1517 the friar Johann Tetzel traveled through German lands selling indulgences, partly to help fund the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. In Catholic teaching of the period, what was an indulgence?
choices: A remission of temporal punishment for sins that had already been confessed
A written permission to commit a future sin without suffering any penalty
A church office bought and sold by wealthy families for their younger sons
A license allowing an ordained priest to marry and still keep his parish
hints: Note the order of events assumed by the doctrine: confession comes first, and the indulgence addresses what remains afterward.

problemText: Protestant reformers summarized part of their position with the phrase 'scripture alone.' What did that phrase claim?
choices: That only clergy trained in Latin should be permitted to read the Bible
That scripture should be printed only in Latin so that translation could not introduce errors
That salvation could be earned by memorizing passages of scripture
That the Bible, rather than church tradition or papal authority, is the final authority in matters of faith
hints: The word 'alone' is doing the work: it names one authority and rules out the others reformers were arguing against.

problemText: A German prince wrote in the 1520s (paraphrased): 'The monasteries in my territory hold a third of the good land and answer to Rome, not to me. If the new preaching frees my lands from Roman courts and Roman collections, then my duty and my own interest point the same direction.' What does this source best illustrate about the Reformation's spread?
choices: Rulers had material and political motives — land, revenue, and independence from Rome — that reinforced the religious argument
German princes were legally barred from holding land for as long as the monasteries in their territories existed
The papacy encouraged princes to seize monastic property as a reform measure to pay for the war against the Turks
Theological disagreement played no part at all in the Reformation's spread, since princes cared about land rather than doctrine
hints: List what the writer says he stands to gain, then ask whether that competes with the religious claim or pushes in the same direction as it.

problemText: Emperor Charles V outlawed Luther at the Diet of Worms in 1521, yet the movement kept growing across the German lands. Which factor best explains why the emperor could not suppress it in its early years?
choices: He had secretly converted and quietly declined to enforce his own edict against Luther and his followers in Germany
He ruled Spain and the Holy Roman Empire at once while fighting France and facing Ottoman pressure, with Vienna besieged in 1529
The Peace of Westphalia had already forbidden emperors from punishing reformers who held the support of their own territorial princes
The German princes were unanimously loyal to Rome and blocked any imperial action that might reduce their own independence
hints: Ask what else was demanding the emperor's armies and money during exactly those decades, and check the dates in each option — Westphalia settled the wars of religion more than a century later, in 1648.

problemText: Luther's break with Rome and Henry VIII's break with Rome each removed a large territory from papal authority. Which statement most accurately distinguishes the origins of the English break from the German one?
choices: Henry acted on John Calvin's teaching of predestination, which had already reached English universities, while Luther rejected predestination outright and stressed free will
Henry's break came first, in 1517, when Parliament rejected papal taxes, and Luther's followed it in 1534, after German princes copied the English example
Luther's break grew out of theological claims about salvation and authority, while Henry's began as a dynastic and jurisdictional dispute over the pope's refusal to annul his marriage
Luther acted with the emperor's protection, since Charles V shared his doubts about indulgences, while Henry acted against the wishes of his own Parliament, which stayed loyal to Rome
hints: Check the dates offered in each option first — one of them reverses the order of two well-known years.
Ask what each man wanted changed: the doctrine of salvation, or the question of who governs the church in his own kingdom.

problemText: Which instrument, Greek in origin and later refined by Islamic astronomers, allowed sailors to estimate their latitude by sighting the sun or the stars?
choices: The lateen sail
The magnetic compass
The caravel
The astrolabe
hints: Two of these are parts of a ship and one is a whole ship; only one is an instrument for measuring angles in the sky.

problemText: Portuguese captains exploring the West African coast needed ships that could return home against the prevailing winds. The caravel solved that problem. Which feature made it possible?
choices: A triangular lateen sail rig, borrowed from Arab and Indian Ocean sailing, that let it sail at an angle into the wind
A steam engine that freed the ship from dependence on wind, letting it hold any course regardless of the weather
A flat bottom that allowed the ship to be hauled overland between rivers and beached on open coasts for repairs and loading
An iron hull heavy enough to push through storms and the strong currents running along the African coast
hints: Sailing out is easy when the wind is behind you; the hard part is the sail shape that lets you make progress toward the wind.

problemText: A Spanish-funded fleet left in 1519 and a single ship completed the first circumnavigation of the globe in 1522. Which statement about that voyage is accurate?
choices: Ferdinand Magellan sailed the entire route himself and returned to Spain in 1522, where he was honored by the king for the feat
Magellan organized and led the fleet but was killed in the Philippines in 1521, and the survivors finished under Juan Sebastian Elcano
The fleet sailed east around Africa and came home by the same route it had gone out, following the path charted by Portuguese captains
Portugal funded the voyage after the Spanish crown refused to support it, hoping to reach the Spice Islands before its rival
hints: Of roughly five ships and more than two hundred men who set out, one ship and a few dozen men came back — ask whether the commander was among them.

problemText: Venice grew enormously rich in the 1400s as the merchant middleman delivering Asian spices into Europe, yet Venetian rulers showed almost no interest in funding voyages around Africa. Which explanation best accounts for that?
choices: Venice had no access to the sea and depended entirely on overland caravans for its trade with Asia
Venetian law forbade its merchants from trading with any non-Christian power, including the rulers of India
Venice profited from its place in the existing route and had no reason to pay for a new one that would bypass it
The Ottoman Empire had granted Venice an exclusive monopoly over Atlantic shipping, so rivals could not legally sail around Africa
hints: Ask who loses if the spice route is replaced, and whether a state usually funds the thing that would put it out of business.

problemText: Royal advisers in both Portugal and Spain repeatedly rejected Christopher Columbus's proposal to reach Asia by sailing west. On what grounds were they right to be skeptical?
choices: They believed the Earth was flat and feared his ships would sail off its edge somewhere in the western ocean
They had calculated the westward distance to Asia as far greater than Columbus claimed, and their figures were correct
They already knew two continents lay in the way and chose not to tell him, keeping the knowledge as a state secret
They objected that no ship of the period could carry enough cannon or soldiers for such a long voyage
hints: Educated Europeans had accepted a spherical Earth for many centuries — so the disagreement had to be about some other quantity.

problemText: A student claims that European ocean voyages after 1450 prove Europe had developed the world's most advanced maritime technology on its own. All four statements below are accurate. Which one most directly challenges that claim?
choices: Portuguese captains pushed a little farther down the African coast each decade for most of a century before finally rounding the Cape of Good Hope in 1488
The Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly claimed lands between Spain and Portugal in 1494 along a line drawn west of the Cape Verde islands
Spanish forces took Tenochtitlan in 1521 and Cusco by 1533, toppling the Aztec and Inca states within a few years
The compass came from China, the astrolabe was Greek and refined by Islamic astronomers, and the lateen sail came from Arab and Indian Ocean sailors
hints: The claim has two parts — most advanced, and on its own. Attack the second part by asking where the equipment came from.
Three options describe what Europeans did with the technology; only one describes who built the technology in the first place.

problemText: Which of these crops originated in the Americas and reached Afro-Eurasia only after 1492?
choices: Wheat
Rice
Potatoes
Sugarcane
hints: Three of these were staples of Old World farming long before 1492; one transformed northern European diets only afterward.

problemText: Historians describe the slavery built in the American colonies as chattel slavery. What did that term mean in law?
choices: Enslaved people were defined in law as property, and that status was inherited by their children
Enslaved people served a fixed term of years and were then released
Enslaved people were legally free but owed rent on the land they worked
Enslavement applied only to prisoners taken in war and ended at the captive's death
hints: The word 'chattel' means movable property — ask what follows for a person's children if the person is legally an object.

problemText: Historians use the phrase 'virgin-soil epidemic' for the outbreaks that struck Indigenous American communities after 1492. What does the phrase describe?
choices: A disease that spreads only through contaminated soil and farmland, infecting people who break ground for new fields
An outbreak in a population with no prior exposure or acquired immunity, so nearly everyone falls ill at once and caregiving collapses
An epidemic confined to farming villages rather than to cities, where crowding had long since spread resistance among the urban residents
A disease that appears once in a population and never returns, because the survivors pass their immunity on to their children
hints: The phrase is about the population, not the ground — ask what it means for a community if no one has met the disease before.

problemText: After 1492 potatoes and maize spread rapidly through northern Europe, China, and West Africa, and historians link them to major population growth in all three regions over the following centuries. Which property of these crops best explains that effect?
choices: They required no labor at all to plant or harvest, so farm families could put their time into other work
They could be stored for decades without spoiling, carrying families safely through years of famine and war
They yielded more calories per acre than most Old World staples and grew on cold, dry, or hilly land unsuited to wheat and rice
They were the first crops anywhere that could be grown from seed, replacing the cuttings and tubers farmers had used before
hints: Population growth needs food, and food needs land — ask what happens when a crop thrives on ground that was previously useless for farming.

problemText: Hernan Cortes besieged the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan in 1521 with only a few hundred Spanish soldiers, and the city fell. Which combination of factors do historians identify as decisive?
choices: Overwhelming Spanish numbers and the absence of any organized Aztec defense, since the Aztec army was away fighting on a distant frontier
A collapse in the price of silver that bankrupted the Aztec state, leaving it unable to pay or feed the warriors defending the city
Terms of the Treaty of Tordesillas that obliged Aztec rulers to surrender their capital to whichever European crown first reached it
A smallpox epidemic that swept the city during the siege, together with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies such as the Tlaxcalans
hints: Start with the arithmetic in the question: a few hundred soldiers cannot besiege a city of that size, so ask who else was fighting and what else was killing people inside the walls.

problemText: Which sequence correctly orders the developments that led colonizers in Spanish and Portuguese America to import enslaved Africans on a mass scale?
choices: Sugar plantations and silver mines demanded labor, then disease and forced labor destroyed the Indigenous workforce, then the Atlantic trade in enslaved Africans expanded to replace it
Enslaved Africans were imported first, their arrival introduced smallpox to the Americas, and the Indigenous population collapsed afterward, leaving plantations dependent on African labor
Indigenous communities refused to grow unfamiliar crops, colonists petitioned the crown for relief, and the crown ordered the importation of Africans as a punishment for that refusal
European factories needed raw cotton, steam-powered ships made the Atlantic crossing cheap, and plantations expanded to supply the mills, which then required far more enslaved workers
hints: Work out the order of three things: the demand for labor, the destruction of the labor force colonizers were already coercing, and the replacement of that labor force.
Check the centuries as well — the sugar and silver boom runs from the 1500s, while steam power and industrial cotton demand belong to the late 1700s and after.
